§3.1: t and k 'have become voiced in initial and intervocalic positions in grammatical morphemes only. They have remained voiceless in lexical stems': PNP *atu 'away from speaker' > adu but *ʔatu 'row' > atu; *te > de 'definite article', *taku > dagu. Gradual: the Muli manuscript (1880) still has ko and ki (p. 528).
§3.1: *foki 'also' > fogi but *foki 'return' > foki; *ke > ge 'you', *ki > gi 'to, towards', *ko > go, *ku > gu 'I', and the embedded pronouns (*kitaaua > -gidaa).

§3.2: 'only one word of Polynesian origin attesting a voiceless nasal': hmaa ~ maa 'be ashamed' (< PPN *maa, at Heo only, perhaps from Drehu). The split of *m and *n proposed after Elbert (1965) by Pawley (1967) and Hollyman (1987: 20) is 'ill-founded'; voiceless nasals come from Iaai loans and are in free variation with voiced ones (p. 529).
§3.2: hnoo ~ noo 'stay' (< PPN *nofo) is the only sure case, perhaps devoicing by metathesis in a borrowed noho > nhoo (p. 529).
